label: Ezra-Nekhemyah — Part 1 — Ezra
summary_plain: Ezra records the return from Babylon after Koresh (Cyrus) of Persia issues his decree: YHWH has charged me to build him a house at Yerushalayim. The exiles who return are listed by family: the children of Yehudah, Binyamin, and the priests and Levites. The temple is rebuilt. Ezra the scribe arrives from Babylon with the Torah of Moshe in his hand. He discovers that the returned exiles have intermarried with the peoples of the land and calls the assembly to separation — to put away the foreign wives and return to the covenant.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Ezra from DSS witnesses (4QEzra, fragmentary) and the Orit Ge'ez. The return from Babylon is critical for understanding post-exilic Israelite identity. Only a fraction of the exiled population returned — primarily from Yehudah (Judah), Binyamin (Benjamin), and Levi. The northern tribes — exiled by Assyria in 722 BCE — did not return. They were already scattered across the Assyrian Empire's territory and beyond, into Africa, Central Asia, and regions the text does not track. The term 'Jew' (Yehudi) originates in this period — it means 'from Yehudah,' one of twelve tribes. The Great Eraser mechanism collapses all twelve tribes into 'Jews,' erasing the ten northern tribes and their descendants entirely. Ezra's genealogy lists (chapters 2 and 8) record only southern tribal families. The Koresh decree (1:1-4) is corroborated by the Cyrus Cylinder (539 BCE, British Museum) — the Persian imperial policy of restoring displaced peoples to their homelands.

key_terms.definition: Ezra 1:1-4: Koresh king of Persia issues the decree allowing the exiled Yehudim to return to Yerushalayim and rebuild the Temple. The decree states: 'YHWH the Creator of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Yerushalayim.' YHWH specifically identifies Koresh in advance through Yesha'yahu — 'my shepherd' — as the instrument of restoration.

The term used throughout Ezra for those who returned from Babylon — members of the southern tribes (Yehudah and Binyamin) with some Levites. The northern tribes (the ten) did not return as a group. This distinction matters for understanding which part of the covenant community reconstituted in the land after the exile.

Ezra 7:6: Ezra is introduced as 'a scribe skilled in the Torah of Moshe which YHWH the Creator of Yisra'el had given.' The scribe (sofer) is the custodian and interpreter of the written Torah. Ezra's role is not primarily priestly (though he is from the priestly line) — it is scribal. He brings the Torah from Babylon to Yehudah.

The return from Babylon described in Ezra 1-2: the first wave under Zerubbavel (approximately 537 BCE), and the second wave under Ezra himself (approximately 458 BCE). The return is modeled on the Exodus: YHWH stirs the spirit of Koresh just as he stirred the spirit of the people to go up to build the Temple.

Ezra 1:7-11: Koresh brings out the vessels that Nevukhadnetzar had taken from the Temple in Yerushalayim — 5,400 articles of gold and silver — and returns them to Sheshbazzar (Zerubbavel). The return of the Temple vessels is a covenant sign: what Babylon stole is restored. The Temple's continuity with the first Temple is established through these vessels.

key_terms.term: The Foundation of the Temple Laid
key_terms.definition: Ezra 3:10-13: when the builders laid the foundation of the restored Temple, the priests and Levites celebrated with shofars and cymbals. The old men who had seen the first Temple wept aloud; the young men shouted for joy. The two sounds — weeping and shouting — could not be distinguished. The moment carried both grief for what was lost and hope for what was beginning.

Ezra 4-5: when the exiles begin building, 'the adversaries of Yehudah and Binyamin' approach and ask to build with them, claiming they also worship YHWH. Zerubbavel refuses. The adversaries then work to discourage and frustrate the building — writing letters to Persian kings accusing the builders of rebellion. The building stops for years during the reign of Artaxerxes.

Ezra 9-10: when Ezra arrives, the officials report that the people, including priests and Levites, have taken foreign wives. Ezra tears his garment, pulls hair from his beard, and sits desolate. His prayer in chapter 9 is a full covenant confession. The covenant community then sends away the foreign wives and their children — a severe covenant action that Ezra receives as YHWH's demand for covenant purity.

Ezra 9:6-15: Ezra's public prayer is one of the most direct covenant confessions in scripture. It opens: 'O my Creator, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads.' Ezra identifies himself with the whole people's guilt — 'we have been in great guilt.' He acknowledges that YHWH has given the community 'a brief moment of favor' in the Persian period but that they have again broken the covenant.

key_terms.term: The Decree of Artaxerxes to Ezra
key_terms.definition: Ezra 7:12-26: Artaxerxes grants Ezra specific authority to inquire about Yehudah and Yerushalayim according to the Torah of YHWH, to appoint judges, to enforce Torah law, and to draw from royal treasury. The decree is remarkably broad. Ezra understands it as YHWH's provision: 'Blessed be YHWH the Creator of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king.'

faq.question: Why does it matter that only southern tribes returned from Babylon?
faq.answer: The return under Koresh and Ezra involved primarily the tribes of Yehudah and Binyamin, with the Levites. The northern tribes (the house of Yosef — Efrayim, Menasheh, and the other eight) had been deported by Ashur approximately 150 years earlier and did not return as a community. This means what reconstituted in the land after the exile was not 'all Yisra'el' — it was the southern remnant. The ten northern tribes remained scattered. This is what Yehezkel's two-sticks prophecy addresses: YHWH promises a future restoration that includes both houses — which had not yet happened at the time of Ezra. The return under Koresh is partial, not complete, covenant restoration.

faq.question: What does the Koresh (Cyrus) decree reveal about YHWH's sovereignty?
faq.answer: YHWH declares through Yesha'yahu (chapters 44-45), written at least 150 years before Koresh lived, that 'Koresh is my shepherd; he will perform all my purpose.' He calls Koresh 'my anointed' — the same word used for the Davidic king. YHWH uses a foreign, non-covenant king as the instrument of covenant restoration. The Koresh decree in Ezra 1 is therefore not evidence of Persian religious pluralism — it is evidence of YHWH's governance of all kingdoms. Koresh's spirit was 'stirred' by YHWH. The same Creator who orchestrated the Exodus through Pharaoh orchestrated the return through Koresh.

faq.question: What happened to the ten northern tribes?
faq.answer: The Assyrian Empire deported the population of the northern kingdom (Yisra'el/Efrayim) in stages between approximately 740-720 BCE. 2 Melakhim 17 describes the deportation: Yisra'el was carried to Ashur and other territories; other peoples were brought in to settle Shomron. No organized return of the ten northern tribes from Assyrian exile is documented in the Tanakh. The community that returned under Koresh was primarily from Yehudah and Binyamin. The scattered northern tribes became what is sometimes called the 'lost tribes' — their fate is addressed in YHWH's future-gathering prophecies (Yehezkel 37, Yesha'yahu 11, Yirmeyahu 31) but not by the return documented in Ezra.

faq.question: What does Ezra's prayer of confession reveal about covenant identity after the exile?
faq.answer: Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 is remarkable for what it identifies: Ezra, who was not himself guilty of intermarriage, prays 'we have been in great guilt' — he absorbs the community's accountability into himself. This is the intercessor's posture that YHWH could not find in Yehezkel 22. Ezra also does not ask YHWH to overlook the violation — he acknowledges YHWH's grace ('a brief moment of favor') while identifying the present crisis as covenant breaking. The prayer does not propose a solution; it places the community in YHWH's hands. The community's response — to send away the foreign wives — comes from them, not from Ezra's prayer. The prayer clears the space for the community to act.

faq.question: Why did Zerubbavel refuse the adversaries' offer to help build?
faq.answer: The adversaries in Ezra 4 claimed to worship YHWH: 'we have been sacrificing to him since the days of Esarhaddon.' But the returned exiles had a specific identity: they were the covenant community whose exile and return was a divine covenant action. Letting in those who claimed covenant standing based on mixed worship (they 'worshipped YHWH and also served their own gods' — 2 Melakhim 17:33) would blur the covenant community's boundaries at the moment of its reconstitution. Zerubbavel's refusal is not ethnic exclusion — it is covenant definition: the community being reconstituted has a specific identity as YHWH's restored covenant people, not a general religious coalition.

faq.question: What does the weeping at the Temple's foundation reveal?
faq.answer: When the Temple's foundation was laid, the older generation wept and the younger shouted for joy. The old men had seen Shelomoh's Temple with its massive stones, cedar, gold, and the visible glory of YHWH. What they saw now was modest in comparison — the foundation of a smaller building being laid in a city still largely in ruins. Their weeping was not despair; it was grief that carried memory. The two sounds mingling — the community could not separate them — captures the texture of covenant restoration: it is simultaneously real hope and carried loss. The prophets (Zekhariah 4:10) had to address this response: 'who has despised the day of small things?'

faq.question: What is the covenant significance of Ezra's role as sofer (scribe)?
faq.answer: Ezra arrives in Yehudah with Torah in hand. His role is not to be a new Moses — it is to establish the written Torah as the community's governing authority. The scribe (sofer) is the person who can read, interpret, and apply the written text. Before Ezra, the Torah existed but its regular communal reading and legal application were not established. After Ezra (Nekhemyah 8), the Torah is read publicly to the whole community for the first time in living memory. Ezra's scribal role is therefore foundational for a covenant community whose identity is inseparable from the written text of YHWH's instruction.

faq.question: What is the significance of the Cyrus Decree for the Hebrew people?
faq.answer: Cyrus king of Persia declares that YHWH the Creator of heaven gave him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build YHWH a house in Yerushalayim — fulfilling Yirmeyahu's prophecy about the 70-year exile and enabling the first return from Babylon.

faq.question: What was Ezra's role and lineage?
faq.answer: Ezra was a scribe skilled in the Torah of Mosheh, descended from Pinkhas son of Aharon the priest. He was a priest and scribe who set his heart to study the Torah of YHWH, to do it, and to teach his statutes in Yisra'el.

faq.question: What crisis did Ezra face regarding mixed marriages?
faq.answer: Ezra was told that the people, including priests and Levites, had not separated from the peoples of the lands and had taken foreign wives. Ezra tore his garments, pulled hair from his head and beard, and sat appalled until evening — then led a great covenant assembly to address the situation.
